Impact of local girth on the SS-packing coloring of kk-saturated subcubic graphs

Ayman El Zein 33footnotemark: 3 Note: Corresponding author. Computer Science Department, University of Sciences and Arts in Lebanon, Beirut, Lebanon; KALMA Laboratory, Faculty of Sciences, Lebanese University, Beirut, Lebanon. email: a.elzein@usal.edu.lb    Maidoun Mortada Note: KALMA Laboratory, Faculty of Sciences, Lebanese University, Baalbek, Lebanon; Basic and Applied Sciences Research, Al Maaref University, Beirut, Lebanon; and Graph Theory and Operation Research, Department of Mathematics and Physics, Lebanese International University (LIU), Beirut, Lebanon. email: maydoun.mortada@liu.edu.lb Note: The two authors contributed equally and are considered co-first authors.
Abstract

For a non-decreasing sequence S=(s1,s2,…,sk)S=(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{k}), an SS-packing coloring of a graph GG is a vertex coloring using the colors s1,s2,…,sks_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{k} such that any two vertices assigned the same color sis_{i} are at distance greater than sis_{i}. A subcubic graph is said to be kk-saturated, for 0≤k≤30\leq k\leq 3, if every vertex of degree 3 is adjacent to at most kk vertices of degree 3. The local girth of a vertex is the length of the smallest cycle containing it. Brešar, Kuenzel, and Rall [Discrete Math. 348(8) (2025), 114477] proved that every claw-free cubic graph is (1,1,2,2)(1,1,2,2)-packing colorable, confirming the conjecture for this family. Equivalently, a claw-free cubic graph is one in which each 33-vertex has local girth 3. Motivated by this observation and by recent progress on SS-packing colorings of kk-saturated subcubic graphs, we study the influence of local girth on their SS-packing colorability. We establish a series of results describing how the parameters of saturation and local girth jointly determine the admissible SS-packing sequences. Sharpness is verified through explicit constructions, and several open problems are posed to delineate the remaining cases.

Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C15
Keywords: graph, coloring, SS-packing coloring, subcubic graph, local girth.

1 Introduction

All graphs considered in this paper are finite, simple, and undirected. For a graph GG, we denote by V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) its vertex and edge sets, respectively. For a vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), we denote by N⁡(x)N(x) the set of the neighbors of xx and by N2​(x)N_{2}(x) the set of vertices at distance exactly two from xx. For a subset X⊆V⁡(G)X\subseteq V(G), we write N⁡[X]=X∪N⁡(X)N[X]=X\cup N(X) for the closed neighborhood of XX. The degree of a vertex xx is denoted by dG​(x)d_{G}(x) (or simply d⁡(x)d(x)), and we write Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) and δ⁡(G)\delta(G) for the maximum and minimum degrees of GG. A vertex vv with d⁡(v)=kd(v)=k is called a kk-vertex. A graph GG is said to be subcubic if Δ⁡(G)≤3\Delta(G)\leq 3 and cubic if dG​(v)=3d_{G}(v)=3 for every vertex vv. A subcubic graph is said to be kk-saturated, for 0≤k≤30\leq k\leq 3, if every vertex of degree 3 is adjacent to at most kk vertices of degree 3. Equivalently, a 33-vertex in a kk-saturated graph has at least 3−k3-k neighbors of degree 2. In a 3-saturated subcubic graph, we call a 3-vertex heavy if all its neighbors are 3-vertices. A 33-saturated subcubic graph is said to be (3,k)(3,k)-saturated, for 0≤k≤30\leq k\leq 3, if each heavy vertex is adjacent to at most kk heavy vertices. This classification, introduced in [15, 16], provides a natural hierarchy of subcubic graphs according to the density of adjacent 33-vertices and will serve as one of the structural parameters in our analysis. A chord in a cycle is an edge joining two vertices that are not adjacent on the cycle.

Given a non-decreasing sequence of positive integers S=(s1,s2,…,sk)S=(s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{k}), an SS-packing coloring of a graph GG is a partition of V⁡(G)V(G) into subsets V1,V2,…,VkV_{1},V_{2},\ldots,V_{k} such that for any two distinct vertices u,v∈Viu,v\in V_{i}, we have d​i​s​tG​(u,v)>sidist_{G}(u,v)>s_{i}. The concept, introduced by Goddard et al. [9], has since inspired intensive research, particularly on graphs of maximum degree three (see the survey [2]). The smallest integer kk such that GG admits a (1,2,…,k)(1,2,\ldots,k)-packing coloring is called the packing chromatic number of GG, denoted χρ​(G)\chi_{\rho}(G). This parameter was introduced by Goddard et al. [9] under the name broadcast chromatic number, who showed that deciding whether χρ​(G)≤4\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 4 is NP-hard. The study of bounding χρ​(G)\chi_{\rho}(G) and χρ​(S​(G))\chi_{\rho}(S(G)), where S⁡(G)S(G) denotes the graph obtained from GG by subdividing every edge, has been the subject of many works [1, 3, 4, 8, 11, 19]. The question of whether χρ\chi_{\rho} is bounded for subcubic graphs was answered negatively by Balogh, Kostochka, and Liu [1], with explicit unbounded constructions later provided in [2]. However, Balogh, Kostochka, and Liu [1] proved that χρ​(S⁡(G))≤8\chi_{\rho}(S(G))\leq 8 for every subcubic graph GG, while Gastineau and Togni [8] raised the question of whether χρ​(S⁡(G))≤5\chi_{\rho}(S(G))\leq 5. This conjecture was later supported by Brešar et al. [4], who proposed that χρ​(S⁡(G))≤5\chi_{\rho}(S(G))\leq 5 holds for all subcubic graphs. Moreover, Gastineau and Togni [19] observed that if a subcubic graph GG is (1,1,2,2)(1,1,2,2)-packing colorable, then it satisfies χρ​(S⁡(G))≤5\chi_{\rho}(S(G))\leq 5.

Several significant results have been obtained on the SS-packing coloring of subcubic graphs. It was recently shown in [13] that every subcubic graph GG admits a (1,1,2,2,3)(1,1,2,2,3)-packing coloring, which implies the general upper bound χρ​(S⁡(G))≤6\chi_{\rho}(S(G))\leq 6 for this class. Later, El Zein and Mortada [6] proved that every subcubic graph with minimum degree less than three is (1,1,2,2)(1,1,2,2)-packing colorable, confirming that shorter SS-sequences suffice in the subcubic case. Their work also established that every connected cubic graph admits a (1,1,2,2,k)(1,1,2,2,k)-packing coloring in which at most one vertex receives color kk, for any k≥3k\geq 3, thereby improving the result of [13]. This line of research continues and unifies earlier contributions by Mortada and Togni, who introduced and systematically developed the study of SS-packing colorings of kk-saturated subcubic graphs [15, 16, 17, 18], as well as by Mortada and El Zein [14], whose recent work further refined the saturation framework. The present paper builds upon these foundations, combining the saturation-based perspective with the newly introduced local girth parameter to obtain a unified theory of SS-packing colorability.

Subsequently, Brešar, Kuenzel, and Rall [5] showed that every claw-free cubic graph is (1,1,2,2)(1,1,2,2)-packing colorable. Their result, obtained through a detailed structural decomposition, revealed the importance of local restrictions in achieving compact SS-packings and inspired the present investigation.

The notion of local girth provides a natural parameter for describing the local cyclic structure of a vertex. For a vertex vv, its local girth, denoted g⁡(v)g(v), is the length of the shortest cycle containing vv, and it is supposed to be ∞\infty if vv belongs to no cycle. A claw-free cubic graph is precisely a cubic graph in which every vertex has local girth 3. Consequently, Brešar, Kuenzel, and Rall [5] admits a natural reformulation in terms of local girth: Every cubic graph in which every vertex has local girth 33 is (1,1,2,2)(1,1,2,2)-packing colorable.

Motivated by this characterization, El Zein and Mortada [7] proved that every subcubic graph such that each 3-vertex has local girth at most 4 is (1,2,2,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable, extending the claw-free case beyond the cubic setting.

In this paper, we unify and extend these two directions—the study based on the saturation level and that guided by the local girth—by analyzing the impact of local girth on the SS-packing coloring of kk-saturated subcubic graphs. We develop a general framework in which the local girth of 33-vertices governs the admissible packing configurations within each saturation class. For a subcubic graph GG, we denote by g3​(G)=max⁡{g⁡(v):dG​(v)=3}g_{3}(G)=\max\{\mathrm{g}(v):d_{G}(v)=3\} the local girth of 3-vertices, that is, the smallest length of a cycle containing any 3-vertex. Our results cover and generalize several known cases in a unified manner.

For clarity and completeness, all the obtained bounds for the SS-packing colorings of kk-saturated subcubic graphs under various local girth constraints are summarized in Table 1. This table highlights the interplay between the two structural parameters—the saturation level and the local girth of 33-vertices—and illustrates how their combination determines the admissible SS-packing sequences. Some of these results hold with exceptions for a small number of specific graphs, which are later identified and treated separately in the corresponding sections. The table also presents the open problems that naturally arise from these results, showing the frontier between proven cases and conjectured extensions. In each case, the presented bounds are proven to be sharp, with explicit constructions provided whenever equality holds.

The proofs rely on a local and constructive analysis guided by the interaction between the saturation level and the local girth of 33-vertices. For each considered class, we identify the structural constraints that determine the admissible SS-packing patterns and verify that these constraints guarantee the existence of the corresponding colorings. The constructive nature of the most of these arguments naturally leads to explicit procedures that can be formulated as efficient algorithms for producing the required SS-packing colorings.

The paper is organized according to the saturation level of the considered subcubic graphs. Section 2 deals with graphs of low saturation (0- and 1-saturated), where the influence of short local cycles on admissible SS-packings is first analyzed. Section 3 focuses on 2-saturated graphs, establishing refined bounds that depend on the interaction between 3-vertices and local girth constraints. Section 4 is devoted to the most intricate case of 3-saturated graphs, where we classify several subclasses and determine optimal SS-packing colorings. Finally, Section 5 provides a synthesis of all obtained results, discusses sharpness and exceptional graphs, and concludes with open problems motivated by the observed connection between local girth and packing colorability.

2 00-Saturated and 11-Saturated

We start by a lemma on graphs having connected components paths and/or cycles.

Lemma 1

Let GG be a connected graph such that Δ⁡(G)≤2\Delta(G)\leq 2. Then,

  • (i)

    GG is (1,1,k)(1,1,k)-packing colorable for every k≥1k\geq 1.

  • (ii)

    GG is (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable unless G=C5G=C_{5},

  • (iii)

    GG is (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable unless G=C5G=C_{5}.

  • (iv)

    GG is (1,2,4,5,k)(1,2,4,5,k)-packing colorable for every k≥6k\geq 6.

Proof.

It is sufficient to suppose that GG is a cycle of order nn. Trivially, (i) holds. Here is the proof of (ii).
Case 1: n=12​m+rn=12m+r for some m≥0m\geq 0 and r∈{0,3,6,9}r\in\{0,3,6,9\}.
Here nn is a multiple of 33. Color the vertices of GG using the sequence 12a​2b​…​12a​2b.12_{a}2_{b}\dots 12_{a}2_{b}.
Case 2: n=12​m+rn=12m+r for some m≥0m\geq 0 and r∈{1,4,7,10}r\in\{1,4,7,10\}.
Here n=3​p+1n=3p+1 for some p≥1p\geq 1. Color the first four vertices by 12a​12b12_{a}12_{b}, then the number of the remaining vertices is a multiple of 33, color them using the sequence 12a​2b​…​12a​2b12_{a}2_{b}\dots 12_{a}2_{b}.
Case 3: n=12​m+2n=12m+2 for some m≥1m\geq 1.
Here n=4​p+2n=4p+2 for some p≥3p\geq 3. Color the first six vertices using the sequence 2a​12b​2a​12b2_{a}12_{b}2_{a}12_{b}, then the number of the remaining vertices is a multiple of 44, color them using the sequence 12a​12b​…​12a​12b12_{a}12_{b}\dots 12_{a}12_{b}.
Case 4: n=12​m+8n=12m+8 for some m≥0m\geq 0.
Here n=4​pn=4p for some p≥2p\geq 2. Use the sequence 12a​12b​…​12a​12b12_{a}12_{b}\dots 12_{a}12_{b}.
Case 5: n=12​m+11n=12m+11 for some m≥0m\geq 0.
Here n=4​p+3n=4p+3 for some p≥2p\geq 2. Color the first three vertices using the sequence 12a​2b12_{a}2_{b}, then the number of the remaining vertices is a multiple of 44, color them using the sequence 12a​12b​…​12a​12b12_{a}12_{b}\dots 12_{a}12_{b}.
Case 6: n=12​m+5n=12m+5 for some m≥1m\geq 1.
Color the first seventeen vertices using the sequence 2b​12a​12b​12a​2b​12a​2b​12a​2b​12a​12_{b}12_{a}12_{b}12_{a}2_{b}12_{a}2_{b}12_{a}2_{b}12_{a}1, then the number of the remaining vertices is a multiple of 1212, color them using the sequence 2b​12a​12b​12a​12b​12a​1​…​2b​12a​12b​12a​12b​12a​12_{b}12_{a}12_{b}12_{a}12_{b}12_{a}1\dots 2_{b}12_{a}12_{b}12_{a}12_{b}12_{a}1.

The proof of (ii) can be extended to a proof of (iii) by recoloring the vertices that are colored by 11 using the colors 2c2_{c} and 2d2_{d} properly. Here is the proof of (iv).
Case 1: n=4​mn=4m for some m≥1m\geq 1.
If mm is even, color the vertices of GG using the sequence 1,2,1,4,1,2,1,5,…1,2,1,4,1,2,1,5,\dots. If mm is odd, color the vertices of GG using the sequence 1,2,1,4,1,2,1,5,…,1,2,1,5,1,2,1,k1,2,1,4,1,2,1,5,\dots,1,2,1,5,1,2,1,k.

The following theorem establishes several results concerning 00- and 11-saturated subcubic graphs in which the local girth of 3-vertices, g3​(⋅)g_{3}(\cdot), is bounded by 44 and 33, respectively.

Theorem 1

Let GG be a subcubic graph that satisfies one of the following:

  • (a)

    GG is 00-saturated and g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4,

  • (b)

    GG is 11-saturated and g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3.

Then, GG is SS-packing colorable, when one of the following holds:

  • (i)

    S=(1,1,3,k)S=(1,1,3,k) for any k≥3k\geq 3,

  • (ii)

    S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3),

  • (iii)

    S=(2,2,2,2,3)S=(2,2,2,2,3) and G≠𝒢1G\neq\mathcal{G}_{1},

  • (iv)

    S=(1,2,3,4,5,k)S=(1,2,3,4,5,k) for any k≥6k\geq 6.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we may suppose that GG is connected. An SS-packing coloring of GG is said to be good if the color 33 is used only for 22-vertices that are adjacent to a 33-vertex and that are in a cycle of order at most g3​(G)g_{3}(G). We will prove, by induction on the number of 33-vertices in GG, that GG has a good SS-packing coloring, except for the following cases, referred to as bad exceptions:

  • (1)

    G=C5G=C_{5} and S=(2,2,2,2,3)S=(2,2,2,2,3),

  • (2)

    G=C5G=C_{5} and S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3),

  • (3)

    G=𝒢1G=\mathcal{G}_{1} and S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3),

  • (4)

    G=𝒢2G=\mathcal{G}_{2} and S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3),

  • (5)

    G=𝒢3G=\mathcal{G}_{3} and S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3).

First, suppose that GG has no 33-vertices. Then, the result follows from Lemma 1. Now, assume that GG contains 33-vertices. Let xx be a 33-vertex and x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} be the neighbors of xx such that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} belong to a smallest cycle containing xx, called CxC_{x}. As GG is ii-saturated, where i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, we may assume that x1x_{1} is a 22-vertex. Let G′=G−x1G^{\prime}=G-x_{1}. Clearly, d​i​s​tG′​(u,v)=d​i​s​tG​(u,v)dist_{G^{\prime}}(u,v)=dist_{G}(u,v) for all u,v∈V⁡(G′)u,v\in V(G^{\prime}). Moreover, G′G^{\prime} is i′i^{\prime}-saturated, where i′≤ii^{\prime}\leq i, while GG is ii-saturated. In addition, g3​(G′)≤g3​(G)g_{3}(G^{\prime})\leq g_{3}(G). Thus, by the induction hypothesis, G′G^{\prime} has a good SS-packing coloring unless G′G^{\prime} and SS form a bad exception.

Case 1: G′G^{\prime} has a good SS-packing coloring.
Let u1u_{1} be a vertex in G′G^{\prime} colored by 33. Then, u1u_{1} is a 22-vertex adjacent to a 33-vertex in G′G^{\prime}, say uu, such that u1u_{1} and uu belong to a cycle in G′G^{\prime} of order at most g3​(G)g_{3}(G), called CuC_{u}.

Claim 1.1

d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)≥2dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})\geq 2.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)=1dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})=1, that is x1x_{1} and u1u_{1} are adjacent. Then, u1u_{1} is a 33-vertex in GG. As GG is ii-saturated, where i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, and u1u_{1} is adjacent to a 33-vertex other than xx, then u1u_{1} is not adjacent to xx. If u1=xu_{1}=x, then GG is not 00-saturated. Hence, g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 and x1x_{1} is adjacent to x2x_{2}. Thus, x2x_{2} is not a 33-vertex in G′G^{\prime} and so u=x3u=x_{3}. Consequently, xx is adjacent to two 33-vertices, x2x_{2} and x3x_{3}, a contradiction. So, u1≠xu_{1}\neq x. Recall that x,x1,x2x,x_{1},x_{2} belong to the cycle CxC_{x} of order at most 44. Now, as x1x_{1} and u1u_{1} are adjacent and since GG is ii-saturated, u1u_{1} belongs to the same cycle, that is Cx=CuC_{x}=C_{u}. As u1u_{1} is neither xx nor x2x_{2}, CxC_{x} is of order 44 and u1u_{1} is adjacent to x2x_{2}. Thus, g3​(G)=4g_{3}(G)=4 and GG is 00-saturated. But u1u_{1} and uu are two adjacent 33-vertices, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 1.2

d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)≥3dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})\geq 3.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)=2dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})=2. Then, x1x_{1} and u1u_{1} have a common neighbor. If u1u_{1} is adjacent to xx and x2x_{2}, that is u=x2u=x_{2}, then GG is not 00-saturated and so g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3. Hence, V⁡(Cu)={x,x2,u1}V(C_{u})=\{x,x_{2},u_{1}\}. Recall that uu is a 33-vertex in G′G^{\prime}, then the neighbor of uu other than u1u_{1} and xx is not x1x_{1}. Thus, CxC_{x} is of order at least 44, a contradiction. Now, if u1u_{1} is adjacent to xx but not to x2x_{2}, then CuC_{u} is of order 44 and so GG is 00-saturated. Thus, x2x_{2} is a 22-vertex. As uu is a 33-vertex in G′G^{\prime}, CxC_{x} is of order at least 55, a contradiction. Similarly, if x2x_{2} is a common neighbor of x1x_{1} and u1u_{1}, we may find a contradiction. Finally, assume that x1x_{1} and u1u_{1} have a common neighbor yy other than xx and x2x_{2}. Then, Cx=x​x1​y​x2C_{x}=xx_{1}yx_{2} and so g3​(G)=4g_{3}(G)=4 and GG is 00-saturated. Hence, x2x_{2} is a 22-vertex. Thus, CuC_{u} is of order at least 55, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 1.3

d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)≥4dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})\geq 4.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)=3dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})=3. Then, there exist a neighbor yy of x1x_{1} and a neighbor zz of u1u_{1} such that yy and zz are adjacent. Note that zz is not adjacent to x1x_{1}. First, suppose that y=xy=x. If z=x2z=x_{2}, then zz is adjacent to a third vertex that belongs to CxC_{x}, and so GG is 11-saturated with g3​(G)≥4g_{3}(G)\geq 4, a contradiction. So, we may assume that z=x3z=x_{3}. As z∈V⁡(Cu)z\in V(C_{u}) and neither x1x_{1} nor x2x_{2} is adjacent to u1u_{1}, zz has a third neighbor, say ww, other than x,x1,x2x,x_{1},x_{2}, such that w∈V⁡(Cu)w\in V(C_{u}). Now, xx and zz are two adjacent 33-vertices. Then, GG is 11-saturated and g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3. Hence, x2x_{2} is a 22-vertex and G=𝒢3G=\mathcal{G}_{3}. In this case, one can check that GG has a good SS-packing coloring unless S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3), which is a bad exception. Now, assume that y≠xy\neq x. If y=x2y=x_{2}, then yy is a 33-vertex and so zz is a 22-vertex. Thus, the order of CuC_{u} is at least 55, a contradiction. Hence, we may assume that y≠x2y\neq x_{2}. Thus, Cx=x​x1​y​x2C_{x}=xx_{1}yx_{2} and GG is 00-saturated. Again, zz is a 22-vertex which leads to a contradiction. ∎

Now, as d​i​s​tG​(x1,u1)≥4dist_{G}(x_{1},u_{1})\geq 4, we can color x1x_{1} by 33 to obtain a good SS-packing coloring of GG.

Case 2: G′G^{\prime} and SS form a bad exception.
If G′=𝒢iG^{\prime}=\mathcal{G}_{i} for some i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}, then GG is not 11-saturated, a contradiction. So, we may assume that G′=C5G^{\prime}=C_{5}. Then, G=𝒢2G=\mathcal{G}_{2} or G=𝒢1G=\mathcal{G}_{1}. If G=𝒢2G=\mathcal{G}_{2} and S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3), then we are in a bad exception. If G=𝒢2G=\mathcal{G}_{2} and S=(2,2,2,2,3)S=(2,2,2,2,3), then GG has an SS-packing coloring (see Figure 2). If G=𝒢1G=\mathcal{G}_{1}, then S=(1,2,2,3)S=(1,2,2,3), and so we are in a bad exception.

We are left with the bad exceptions that are represented in Figure 2. ∎

As corollaries, the studied graphs have a bounded packing chromatic number.

Corollary 1

If GG is a 00-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4, then χρ​(G)≤6\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 6.

Corollary 2

If GG is a 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3, then χρ​(G)≤6\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 6.

Now, we study 11-saturated subcubic graphs such that g3​(⋅)g_{3}(\cdot) is bounded by 44.

Theorem 2

Every 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

A (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring using the colors 1,2a,2b,2c1,2_{a},2_{b},2_{c} is said to be good if the color 2c2_{c} is used only to color some 22-vertices that belong to a cycle of order at most 44. We will prove that every 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 has a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring. On the contrary, let GG be a counter-example of minimum order. Clearly, GG contains a 33-vertex. Let xx be a 33-vertex. First, suppose that g​(x)=3\text{g}(x)=3. Let yy be a neighbor of xx such that d⁡(y)=2d(y)=2 and yy belongs to a cycle of order 33. Clearly, G−yG-y is a 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G−y)≤4g_{3}(G-y)\leq 4. Then, G−yG-y has a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring. Moreover, yy is at a distance of at least 33 from any 22-vertex that belongs to a cycle of order 33. Thus, one can color yy by 2c2_{c} in order to obtain a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. Now, assume that g​(x)=4\text{g}(x)=4. Let y1,y2,y3y_{1},y_{2},y_{3} be the vertices in the cycle of order 44 that contains xx such that y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} are adjacent to xx. If d⁡(y1)=d⁡(y2)=2d(y_{1})=d(y_{2})=2, then in a similar way as above, one can extend a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of G−y1G-y_{1} to GG to obtain a contradiction. So, we may assume that d⁡(y1)=3d(y_{1})=3 and d⁡(y2)=2d(y_{2})=2. Clearly, y3y_{3} is a 22-vertex. Let G′=G−{y2,y3}G^{\prime}=G-\{y_{2},y_{3}\}. Again, G′G^{\prime} is 11-saturated such that g3​(G′)≤4g_{3}(G^{\prime})\leq 4. Then, G′G^{\prime} has a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring. Moreover, y2y_{2} and y3y_{3} are at a distance of at least 33 from any 22-vertex other than them that are in a cycle of order of at most 44. Now, obviously xx or y1y_{1} is not colored by 11. Without loss of generality, suppose that xx is not colored by 11. Color y2y_{2} by 11 and y3y_{3} by 2c2_{c} in order to obtain a good (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

3 22-Saturated

In this section, we prove three results. We start by a lemma about the structure of a 22-saturated subcubic graph that will be a minimum counter example for the three results if they are supposed to be false. Then, we introduce two easy lemmas that will be useful in the coloring of the graphs in the main results.

Lemma 2

Let GG be a connected 22-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3, δ⁡(G)=2\delta(G)=2, Δ⁡(G)=3\Delta(G)=3, GG contains no diamond, and for every cycle CC in GG we have V⁡(G)≠N⁡[C]V(G)\neq N[C]. Then, GG contains a 22-packing YY such that G−YG-Y is a set of disjoint paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha} of order at least 44, unless PiP_{i} contains a 22-vertex that belongs to a triangle, satisfying the following for all x∈Pix\in P_{i} and y∈Pjy\in P_{j}, i≠ji\neq j:

  • (i)

    d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3 whenever xx and yy are interior vertices,

  • (ii)

    d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3 whenever xx and yy are ends.

Proof.

We will study the structure of GG.

Claim 2.1

Let CC be a cycle and x​yxy be a chord in CC. Then, d​i​s​tC​(x,y)=2dist_{C}(x,y)=2.

Proof.

As x​yxy is a chord in CC, d​i​s​tC​(x,y)≥2dist_{C}(x,y)\geq 2. Suppose to the contrary that d​i​s​tC​(x,y)≥3dist_{C}(x,y)\geq 3. Let x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} be the neighbors of xx in CC. Hence, x1​x2∈E⁡(G)x_{1}x_{2}\in E(G). Thus, the three neighbors of xx are 33-vertices, a contradiction. ∎

A cycle is said to be good if its order is at least 44 and it contains no chords.

Claim 2.2

Let CC be a good cycle and x∈V⁡(G)∖V⁡(C)x\in V(G)\setminus V(C) such that N⁡(x)∩N⁡(C)≠∅N(x)\cap N(C)\neq\emptyset. Then, |N⁡(x)∩V⁡(C)|=2|N(x)\cap V(C)|=2 and the two neighbors of xx in CC are adjacent in CC.

Proof.

Let y∈N⁡(x)∩V⁡(C)y\in N(x)\cap V(C) and let y1,y2y_{1},y_{2} be the neighbors of yy in CC. As CC is good, y1​y2∉E⁡(G)y_{1}y_{2}\notin E(G). Then, either xx is adjacent to y1y_{1} or y2y_{2}. As GG is 22-saturated, xx cannot be adjacent to both y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}. The result follows. ∎

If CC is a good cycle and x∈V⁡(G)∖V⁡(C)x\in V(G)\setminus V(C) such that N⁡(x)∩V⁡(C)≠∅N(x)\cap V(C)\neq\emptyset, then xx is said to be CC-attached.

Claim 2.3

Let CC be a good cycle and x,yx,y be CC-attached vertices. Denote by x1,x2x_{1},x_{2} (resp., y1,y2y_{1},y_{2}) the neighbors of xx (resp., yy) that belong to CC such that x1,x2,y1,y2x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2} are in this order in CC (i.e., x1​x2​v1​…​vk​y1​y2x_{1}x_{2}v_{1}\dots v_{k}y_{1}y_{2} is a path in CC, for some vertices v1,…,vkv_{1},\dots,v_{k}). Then,

  • (i)

    If xx is a 33-vertex, then d​i​s​tG​(x1,y1)≥3dist_{G}(x_{1},y_{1})\geq 3.

  • (ii)

    If xx and yy are 22-vertices, then d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3.

Proof.

Note that x1,x2,y1,y2x_{1},x_{2},y_{1},y_{2} are 33-vertices. Let x1′x^{\prime}_{1} and x2′x^{\prime}_{2} be the third neighbors of x1x_{1} and x2x_{2}, respectively. First, suppose that xx is a 33-vertex. Here, x1′x^{\prime}_{1} and x2′x^{\prime}_{2} are 22-vertices. Then, x1′x^{\prime}_{1} and x2′x^{\prime}_{2} are distinct from y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}. Moreover, xx is not adjacent to y1y_{1}. Thus, x1x_{1} and y1y_{1} are neither adjacent nor have a common neighbor. Therefore, d​i​s​tG​(x1,y1)≥3dist_{G}(x_{1},y_{1})\geq 3. Now, assume that xx and yy are 22-vertices. Clearly, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are different from y1y_{1} and y2y_{2}. Thus, xx and yy are neither adjacent nor have a common neighbor. Therefore, d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3. ∎

Claim 2.4

Let CC be a good cycle and xx be a CC-attached 33-vertex. Denote by x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} the neighbors of xx such that x1,x2∈V⁡(C)x_{1},x_{2}\in V(C). Let a,b,ca,b,c be three vertices that form a triangle in G−V⁡(C)G-V(C). Then, d​i​s​tG​(x1,a)≥3dist_{G}(x_{1},a)\geq 3.

Proof.

Recall that x3x_{3} is a 22-vertex. Then, x3≠ax_{3}\neq a. Similarly, the neighbor of x1x_{1} in CC other than x2x_{2} is a 22-vertex. Thus, x1x_{1} and aa have no common neighbors. The result follows. ∎

Claim 2.5

If GG contains a cycle of order at least 44, then GG contains a good cycle.

Proof.

Let CC be a cycle of order at least 44. If CC has no chords, then we are done. Otherwise, let x​yxy be a chord in CC. By Claim 2.1, d​i​s​tC​(x,y)=2dist_{C}(x,y)=2. As GG contains no diamond, the order of CC is at least 55. Assume that C=v1​v2​…​vn​v1C=v_{1}v_{2}\dots v_{n}v_{1} such that v1​v3v_{1}v_{3} is a chord. Let vi1​vi1+2,…,vir​vir+2v_{i_{1}}v_{i_{1}+2},\dots,v_{i_{r}}v_{i_{r}+2} be the other chords in CC such that i1<⋯<iri_{1}<\dots<i_{r}, if they exist. Then, the cycle v1​v3​…​vi1​vi1+2​…​vir​vir+2​…​v1v_{1}v_{3}\dots v_{i_{1}}v_{i_{1}+2}\dots v_{i_{r}}v_{i_{r}+2}\dots v_{1} is a good cycle in GG. ∎

Let C1C_{1} be a good cycle in GG and G1=G−V⁡(C1)G_{1}=G-V(C_{1}). Recursively, for i≥1i\geq 1, define CiC_{i} as a good cycle in Gi−1G_{i-1} and GiG_{i} to be Gi−1−V⁡(Ci)G_{i-1}-V(C_{i}). This definition ends at some p≥2p\geq 2, where GpG_{p} does not contain a good cycle. Note that if GG contains no good cycle, then GG contains no cycles of order at least 44. In this case, we may assume that Gp=GG_{p}=G.

If there exists i∈{1,…,p}i\in\{1,\dots,p\} such that every CiC_{i}-attached vertex is a 22-vertex, then V⁡(G)=N⁡[Ci]V(G)=N[C_{i}], a contradiction. So, we may assume that, for every i∈{1,…,p}i\in\{1,\dots,p\}, there exists a CiC_{i}-attached 33-vertex. Let i∈{1,…,p}i\in\{1,\dots,p\}. Let AiA_{i} be the set of CiC_{i}-attached 22-vertices. Let x1i,…,xkiix^{i}_{1},\dots,x^{i}_{k_{i}} be the CiC_{i}-attached 33-vertices. Denote by yj,zjy_{j},z_{j} the neighbors of xjix^{i}_{j} that belong to CiC_{i}, for every j∈{1,…,ki}j\in\{1,\dots,k_{i}\}, and suppose that y1,z1,y2,z2,…,yki,zkiy_{1},z_{1},y_{2},z_{2},\dots,y_{k_{i}},z_{k_{i}} appear in this order on CiC_{i}. Let Bi={y1,…,yki}B_{i}=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{k_{i}}\} and OPENX=⋃1≤i≤p(Ai∪Bi))X=\bigcup_{1\leq i\leq p}(A_{i}\cup B_{i})). By Claim 2.3 and Claim 2.4, XX is a 22-packing. Note that if GG contains no good cycles, XX is an empty set that is supposed a 22-packing also.

As GpG_{p} contains no good cycle, every cycle in GpG_{p} is a triangle. Let D1D_{1} be the set formed by exactly one 22-vertex from every triangle in GpG_{p} that contains a 22-vertex. Clearly, X∪D1X\cup D_{1} is a 22-packing. Now, let Gp1G_{p}^{1} be the graph obtained by removing the vertices of every triangle containing a 22-vertex from GpG_{p}. Note that every cycle in Gp1G_{p}^{1} is a triangle formed by three 33-vertices. Moreover, every neighbor of a vertex in a cycle in Gp1G_{p}^{1}, outside the cycle, is a 22-vertex. Now, we will pick a 33-vertex from every cycle in Gp1G_{p}^{1} in order to form a set D2D_{2}. The set Y:=X∪D1∪D2Y:=X\cup D_{1}\cup D_{2} will be a 22-packing that we are aiming for.

Claim 2.6

The set D2D_{2} exists such that YY is a 22-packing.

Proof.

A tt-vertex is a 33-vertex that lies in a triangle in Gp1G_{p}^{1}. Let xx be a tt-vertex. Consider the BFS tree TT of xx. Let x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} be the neighbors of xx such that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are adjacent. Let D2={x}D_{2}=\{x\} for the moment, then we will add vertices to D2D_{2}. A tt-vertex is said to be good if its father in TT is a 22-vertex. Otherwise, it is said to be bad. Note that every triangle in Gp1G_{p}^{1} is formed by a good tt-vertex and two bad tt-vertices. Add to D2D_{2} every good tt-vertex that belongs to the branch of TT of root x1x_{1} (resp., x2x_{2}). Note that the distance between any two vertices in D2D_{2} is at least 33 in TT. Moreover, as Gp1G_{p}^{1} contains no cycle of order at least 44, the distance between every vertex in D2D_{2} is also at least 33 in GG. Now, add to D2D_{2} a bad tt-vertex among every pair of adjacent bad tt-vertices in the branch of TT of root x3x_{3}. It is easy to check that D2D_{2} is a 22-packing. Moreover, every vertex in D2D_{2} is at a distance of at least 33 from every vertex in X∪D1X\cup D_{1}. Note that if TT does not contain every tt-vertex in Gp1G_{p}^{1}, we can consider several BFS trees in the same way. ∎

By the definition of YY, G−YG-Y is a set of disjoint paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha}.

Claim 2.7

The path PiP_{i} is of order at least 44 for every i∈{1,…,α}i\in\{1,\dots,\alpha\} unless PiP_{i} contains a 22-vertex that belongs to a triangle..

Proof.

Let i∈{1,…,α}i\in\{1,\dots,\alpha\}. There exists x∈Pix\in P_{i} such that xx has a neighbor y∈Yy\in Y. Indeed, otherwise, Δ⁡(G)≤2\Delta(G)\leq 2. Let zz be the other neighbor of yy that belongs to PiP_{i}. If yy is a 33-vertex, then xx (resp., zz) is adjacent to a 22-vertex xix_{i} (resp., ziz_{i}) that belongs to PiP_{i}. Then, PiP_{i} is of order at least 44. Otherwise, yy is a 22-vertex. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that xx is a 33-vertex. Let x1x_{1} be the neighbor of xx other than yy and zz. If x1x_{1} is a 33-vertex, then x1x_{1} is contained in a triangle that one of its vertices is a vertex in YY and the last vertex belongs to PiP_{i}. Thus, PiP_{i} is of order at least 44. If x1x_{1} is a 22-vertex, then the neighbor of x1x_{1} other than xx belongs to PiP_{i}. Hence, PiP_{i} is of order at least 44 unless zz is a 22-vertex. Finally, if x1x_{1} is a 11-vertex, then, as V⁡(G)≠N⁡[x​y​z]V(G)\neq N[xyz], zz is a 33-vertex and has a neighbor that belongs to PiP_{i}. The result follows. ∎

Now, if x∈Yx\in Y is a 33-vertex, then xx is contained in a triangle of 33-vertices. Moreover, if x∈Yx\in Y is a 22-vertex, then xx is contained in a triangle. Now, let x∈Pix\in P_{i} and y∈Pjy\in P_{j}, i≠ji\neq j, be two interior vertices. Suppose to the contrary that xx and yy have a common neighbor zz. Clearly, z∈Yz\in Y. If zz is a 22-vertex, then xx and yy are adjacent, a contradiction. So, zz is a 33-vertex. Thus, zz is contained in a triangle of 33-vertices. Without loss of generality, suppose that yy is contained in that triangle and let uu be the third vertex of the triangle. As u≠xu\neq x and GG is 22-saturated, xx is a 22-vertex. Then, xx is an end of PiP_{i}, a contradiction. Therefore, d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3.

Finally, let x∈Pix\in P_{i} and y∈Pjy\in P_{j}, i≠ji\neq j, be two ends. Suppose to the contrary that xx and yy have a common neighbor zz. Again, z∈Yz\in Y. If zz is a 22-vertex, then xx and yy are adjacent, a contradiction. So, zz is a 33-vertex. Thus, zz is contained in a triangle of 33-vertices. Without loss of generality, suppose that yy is contained in that triangle and let u,vu,v be other neighbors of yy. As YY is a 22-packing, uu and vv are not in YY. Then, u,v∈Pju,v\in P_{j} and yy is not an end of PjP_{j}, a contradiction. Therefore, d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3. ∎

The following two lemmas are trivial.

Lemma 3

Let P=v1​…​vnP=v_{1}\dots v_{n} be a path. If n≥3n\geq 3, then PP has a (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing coloring such that v1v_{1} and vnv_{n} are colored by 11.

Lemma 4

Let P=v1​…​vnP=v_{1}\dots v_{n} be a path. If n≥4n\geq 4, then PP has a (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing coloring such that v1v_{1} and vnv_{n} are colored by the same color and neither of v2,…,vn−1v_{2},\dots,v_{n-1} is colored by that color.

Theorem 3

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, let GG be a counter-example of minimum order. Obviously, GG is connected and contains a 33-vertex.

Claim 3.1

We have δ⁡(G)=2\delta(G)=2.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a vertex uu in GG such that d⁡(u)=1d(u)=1. The graph G−uG-u is 22-saturated subcubic such that g3​(G−u)=3g_{3}(G-u)=3. Then, G−uG-u is (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable. Hence, either 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} is not assigned to the neighbor of uu. By coloring uu using the appropriate color 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} we obtain a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 3.2

GG contains no diamond.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that GG contains a diamond and let x1,x2,x3,x4x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} be the vertices of a diamond such that x1​x3x_{1}x_{3} is a chord. As GG is connected and x1x_{1} and x3x_{3} are 33-vertices, either x2x_{2} or x4x_{4} has a neighbor outside the diamond. Without loss of generality, suppose that x2x_{2} is adjacent to a vertex yy outside the diamond. As GG is 22-saturated, x4x_{4} and yy are 22-vertices. consider a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of G−{x1,x2,x3,x4,y}G-\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},y\}. Clearly, yy has one colored neighbor. Then, either 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} is not assigned to its colored neighbor, say 1a1_{a}. Color y,x1,x2,x3,x4y,x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} by 1a,1a,1b,2,1b1_{a},1_{a},1_{b},2,1_{b}, respectively. We obtain a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 3.3

If CC is a cycle, then V⁡(G)≠N⁡[C]V(G)\neq N[C].

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a cycle CC such that V⁡(G)=N⁡[C]V(G)=N[C]. If CC is an even cycle, then we can color the vertices of CC by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b}. The vertices in N⁡(C)N(C) are at a distance of at least 33 from each other, then we can color them by 22 to obtain a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring, a contradiction. Now, assume that CC is an odd cycle. Then, CC contains a 22-vertex. Let C=v1​v2​…​vkC=v_{1}v_{2}\dots v_{k} such that v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} are 33-vertices and v3v_{3} is a 22-vertex. Let x1,…,xmx_{1},\dots,x_{m} be the vertices in N⁡(C)N(C) such that x1x_{1} is adjacent to v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}. Clearly, v2v_{2} is at a distance of at least 33 from any vertex among x2,…,xmx_{2},\dots,x_{m}. Color the vertices v2,x2,…,xmv_{2},x_{2},\dots,x_{m} by 22. The remaining vertices induce a path. Then, we can color the remaining vertices by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b}. We obtain a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Now, by Lemma 2, GG contains a 22-packing YY such that G−YG-Y is a set of disjoint paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha}. Color the vertices of P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha} by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b} to obtain a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Theorem 4

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, let GG be a counter-example of minimum order. Obviously, GG is connected and contains a 33-vertex.

Claim 4.1

δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2.

Proof.

Suppose, to the contrary, that there exists a vertex xx of degree one. Let yy be its (unique) neighbor. By minimality of GG, the graph G−xG-x admits a (1,23)(1,2^{3})-packing coloring with palette {1,2a,2b,2c}\{1,2_{a},2_{b},2_{c}\}. If yy is not colored 11, then color xx by 11 and so the coloring is extended to GG, a contradiction. Otherwise, yy has color 11; pick i∈{a,b,c}i\in\{a,b,c\} such that no vertex at distance 2 from xx has color 2i2_{i} (one exists because at most two vertices are at distance 2 from xx). Color xx by 2i2_{i}, which preserves all packing constraints. This extends the coloring to GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 4.2

GG contains no diamond.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that GG contains a diamond and let x1,x2,x3,x4x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} be the vertices of a diamond such that x1​x3x_{1}x_{3} is a chord. As GG is connected and x1x_{1} and x3x_{3} are 33-vertices, either x2x_{2} or x4x_{4} has a neighbor outside the diamond. Without loss of generality, suppose that x2x_{2} is adjacent to a vertex yy outside the diamond. As GG is 22-saturated, x4x_{4} and yy are 22-vertices. consider a (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing coloring of G−{x1,x2,x3,x4,y}G-\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4},y\}. Clearly, yy has one colored neighbor, say zz. If zz is colored by 11, then at least one of the colored neighbors of zz are not colored by a color 22, say 2a2_{a}. Now, color y,x1,x2,x3,x4y,x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} by 2a,2b,1,2c,12_{a},2_{b},1,2_{c},1, respectively. We obtain a (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. Otherwise, zz is colored by a color 22, say 2a2_{a}. Color y,x1,x2,x3,x4y,x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} by 1,1,2b,2c,2a1,1,2_{b},2_{c},2_{a}, respectively. Again, GG is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 4.3

If CC is a cycle, then V⁡(G)≠N⁡[C]V(G)\neq N[C].

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a cycle CC such that V⁡(G)=N⁡[C]V(G)=N[C]. If CC is of order 55, it can be easily checked that GG is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring, which is a contradiction. Otherwise, CC is not of order 55. Then, by Lemma 1, CC has a (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing coloring using the colors 1,2a,2b1,2_{a},2_{b}. By coloring the vertices of N⁡(C)N(C) by 2c2_{c} we obtain a (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Now, by Lemma 2, GG contains a 22-packing YY such that G−YG-Y is a set of disjoint paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha} of order at least 44 such that d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3 for all interior vertices x∈Pix\in P_{i} and y∈Pjy\in P_{j}, i≠ji\neq j. By Lemma 3, one can color the vertices of the paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha} by 1,2a,2b1,2_{a},2_{b} such that the ends of them are colored by 11. We obtain a (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Theorem 5

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, let GG be a counter-example of minimum order. Obviously, GG is connected and contains a 33-vertex.

Claim 5.1

δ⁡(G)≥2\delta(G)\geq 2.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a vertex uu in GG such that d⁡(u)=1d(u)=1. The graph G−uG-u is 22-saturated subcubic such that g3​(G−u)=3g_{3}(G-u)=3. Then, G−uG-u is (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable. As the number of vertices that are at a distance of at most 22 from uu is at most 33, one can find a color 2i2_{i} for uu that extends the (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring to GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 5.2

GG contains no diamond.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that GG contains a diamond and let x1,x2,x3,x4x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} be the vertices of a diamond such that x1​x3x_{1}x_{3} is a chord. As GG is connected and x1x_{1} and x3x_{3} are 33-vertices, either x2x_{2} or x4x_{4} has a neighbor outside the diamond. Without loss of generality, suppose that x2x_{2} is adjacent to a vertex yy outside the diamond. As GG is 22-saturated, x4x_{4} and yy are 22-vertices. consider a (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring of G−{x1,x2,x3,x4}G-\{x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}\}. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that yy and its colored neighbor are colored by 2a2_{a} and 2b2_{b}, respectively. Color x1,x2,x3,x4x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4} by 2c,2d,2e,2b2_{c},2_{d},2_{e},2_{b}, respectively. We obtain a (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 5.3

If CC is a cycle, then V⁡(G)≠N⁡[C]V(G)\neq N[C].

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a cycle CC such that V⁡(G)=N⁡[C]V(G)=N[C]. If CC is of order 55, it can be easily checked that GG is (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring, which is a contradiction. Otherwise, CC is not of order 55. Then, by Lemma 1, CC has a (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing coloring using the colors 2a,2b,2c,2d2_{a},2_{b},2_{c},2_{d}. By coloring the vertices of N⁡(C)N(C) by 2e2_{e} we obtain a (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Now, by Lemma 2, GG contains a 22-packing YY such that G−YG-Y is a set of disjoint paths P1,…,PαP_{1},\dots,P_{\alpha} of order at least 44, unless PiP_{i} contains a 22-vertex that belongs to a triangle, satisfying the following for all x∈Pix\in P_{i} and y∈Pjy\in P_{j}, i≠ji\neq j:

  • (i)

    d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3 whenever xx and yy are interior vertices,

  • (ii)

    d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥3dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 3 whenever xx and yy are ends.

Suppose that P1,…,PβP_{1},\dots,P_{\beta} are of order at least 44 and Pβ+1,…,PαP_{\beta+1},\dots,P_{\alpha} are of order 33. By Lemma 4, one can color the vertices of the paths P1,…,PβP_{1},\dots,P_{\beta} by 2a,2b,2c,2d2_{a},2_{b},2_{c},2_{d} such that only the ends of them are colored by 2a2_{a}. In addition, color the vertices of Pβ+1,…,PαP_{\beta+1},\dots,P_{\alpha} by 2a,2b,2c2_{a},2_{b},2_{c} such that the end tat does not belong to a triangle is colored by 2a2_{a}. Color the vertices of YY by 2e2_{e} to obtain a (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

4 33-Saturated

As a Corollary of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5, we can deduce the following.

Corollary 3

Every (3,0)(3,0)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,2,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable and (2,2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

Let GG be a (3,0)(3,0)-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 and let x1,…,xsx^{1},\dots,x^{s} be the heavy vertices of GG. Let i∈{1,…,s}i\in\{1,\dots,s\}. We denote bye x1i,x2i,x3ix^{i}_{1},x^{i}_{2},x^{i}_{3} the neighbors of xix^{i} such that x1ix^{i}_{1} and x2ix^{i}_{2} are adjacent. We denote by yiy^{i} and ziz^{i} the neighbors of x3ix^{i}_{3} such that yiy^{i} is a 22-vertex. Obviously, yiy^{i} and ziz^{i} are adjacent. If is clear that, for every distinct integers i,j∈{1,…,s}i,j\in\{1,\dots,s\}, we have d​i​s​tG​(yi,yj)≥3dist_{G}(y^{i},y^{j})\geq 3. Moreover, the graph G′G^{\prime} obtained by deleting the vertices y1,…,ysy^{1},\dots,y^{s} from GG is 22-saturated such that g3​(G′)=3g_{3}(G^{\prime})=3. By Theorem 4 (resp., Theorem 5), G′G^{\prime} is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable (resp., (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable). Color the vertices of G′G^{\prime} by 1,2b,2c,2d1,2_{b},2_{c},2_{d} (resp., 2b,2c,2d,2e,2f2_{b},2_{c},2_{d},2_{e},2_{f}) and the vertices y1,…,ysy^{1},\dots,y^{s} by 2a2_{a} in order to obtain a (1,2,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring (resp., (2,2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring) of GG. ∎

Below, we study the (1,1,2,k)(1,1,2,k)-packing colorings for (3,0)(3,0)- and (3,1)(3,1)-saturated subcubic graphs.

Theorem 6

Let GG be a (3,i)(3,i)-saturated subcubic graph, 0≤i≤10\leq i\leq 1, such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3, then:

  1. 1.

    GG is (1,1,2,4)(1,1,2,4)-packing colorable if i=0i=0.

  2. 2.

    GG is (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-packing colorable if i=1i=1.

Proof.

Let GG be a (3,i)(3,i)-saturated subcubic graph, 0≤i≤10\leq i\leq 1, such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3. For i=0i=0, we will prove GG has a (1,1,2,4)(1,1,2,4)-packing coloring, and for i=1i=1 we will prove GG has a (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-packing coloring. Without loss of generality, suppose that GG is a connected graph.

Our plan is to prove the existence of a 2-packing XX and a 4-packing (resp., 3-packing) YY in GG if i=0i=0 (resp., i=1i=1) such that the subgraph induced by V⁡(G)∖(X∪Y)V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y) is a bipartite one.

A 3-vertex xx is said to be rich if xx is contained in two triangles. Let xx be a rich vertex and let x1x_{1}, x2x_{2} and x3x_{3} be the neighbors of xx. As xx is rich, then one of its neighbors is also a rich vertex; assume this neighbor is x1x_{1}. Since GG is (3,i)(3,i)-saturated with i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, neither x2x_{2} nor x3x_{3} can be rich. In fact, if x2x_{2} is a rich vertex, then x2​x3∈E⁡(G)x_{2}x_{3}\in E(G) and so xx and its neighbors are all heavy vertices, a contradiction. Moreover, if GG is (3,1)(3,1)-saturated and if x2x_{2} and x3x_{3} are 3-vertices, then both x2x_{2} and x3x_{3} are non-heavy vertices.

For each vertex xx in GG, we define the weight of xx, w⁡(x)w(x), such that
w⁡(x)={k1if x is a 2-vertex or a rich 3-vertexk2if x is a non heavy 3-vertex and not richk3if x is a heavy 3-vertex and not rich.w(x)=\begin{cases}k_{1}&\text{if $x$ is a 2-vertex or a rich 3-vertex}\\ k_{2}&\text{if $x$ is a non heavy 3-vertex and not rich}\\ k_{3}&\text{if $x$ is a heavy 3-vertex and not rich.}\end{cases}

with k1k_{1}, k2k_{2}, k3k_{3} are real numbers satisfying k1>k2>k3k_{1}>k_{2}>k_{3} and k1>2​k3k_{1}>2k_{3}.

Let X,Y⊆V⁡(G)X,\;Y\subseteq V(G) such that XX and YY are disjoint. For a packing pair (X,Y)(X,Y), we define θ⁡(X,Y)\theta(X,Y) to be the sum of the weights of the vertices in X∪YX\cup Y, and γ⁡(X,Y)\gamma(X,Y) to be the number of triangles in the subgraph G⁡[V⁡(G)∖(X∪Y)]G[V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)]. The packing pair (X,Y)(X,Y) is said to be a maximum packing pair if θ⁡(X,Y)\theta(X,Y) is maximum. Let (X,Y)(X,Y) be a maximum packing pair such that γ⁡(X,Y)\gamma(X,Y) is minimum. Claim 6.1

Thus, the neighbor of uu other than xx and yy if exists is a 2-vertex. Besides, this neighbor if exists is not in XT∪YTX^{T}\cup Y^{T} since it is not contained in a cycle in G′G^{\prime}.

    The result here follows directly from (1) and (2).

∎

Consequently, for i=1i=1, we get that (XT,Y1T)(X^{T},Y_{1}^{T}) is an extension packing pair of (X,Y)(X,Y) with ϕ⁡(X1t,YT)<ϕ⁡(XT,YT)\phi(X_{1}^{t},Y^{T})<\phi(X^{T},Y^{T}), where Y1T=YT∪{z}Y_{1}^{T}=Y^{T}\cup\{z\}, a contradiction. We proceed with i=0i=0. Set C=v1​…​v2​k+1C=v_{1}\dots v_{2k+1} for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. If each vertex in N⁡(C)∩(XT∪YT)N(C)\cap(X^{T}\cup Y^{T}) is a 2-vertex, then G=N⁡[C]G=N[C] and so it can be easily shown that GG is (1,1,2,4)(1,1,2,4)-packing colorable. Else, let xx be a vertex on CC such that the neighbor of xx in XT∪YTX^{T}\cup Y^{T} is a 3-vertex and let uu be this neighbor. Let yy be the neighbor of xx on CC such that u​x​yuxy is a triangle. Since GG is (3,0)(3,0)-saturated, then either the neighbor of xx or of yy on CC is a 2-vertex. Without loss of generality, suppose that the neighbor of xx on CC is a 2-vertex. By Claim 6.3, each neighbor of a vertex on CC in V⁡(G)∖CV(G)\setminus C is in XT∪YTX^{T}\cup Y^{T}, then each cycle passing through uu in G∖(X1T∪YT)G\setminus(X_{1}^{T}\cup Y^{T}) should pass through xx and yy, where X1T=XT∖{u}.X_{1}^{T}=X^{T}\setminus\{u\}. Let X′=(X∖{u})∪{x}X^{\prime}=(X\setminus\{u\})\cup\{x\}, then (X′,Y)(X^{\prime},Y) is a packing pair with θ⁡(X′,Y)≥θ⁡(X,Y)\theta(X^{\prime},Y)\geq\theta(X,Y). Besides, (X1T∪{x},YT)(X_{1}^{T}\cup\{x\},Y^{T}) is an extension packing pair of (X′,Y)(X^{\prime},Y) with ϕ⁡(X1T∪{x},YT)=ϕ⁡(XT,YT)−1\phi(X_{1}^{T}\cup\{x\},Y^{T})=\phi(X^{T},Y^{T})-1 since CC no more exists in G∖(X1T∪{x},YT)G\setminus(X_{1}^{T}\cup\{x\},Y^{T}), a contradiction.

The obtained coloring is a (1,1,2,4)(1,1,2,4)-packing coloring if i=0i=0 and (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-packing coloring if i=1i=1. ∎

Finally, we study the (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorability of (3,2)(3,2)-saturated subcubic graphs.

Theorem 7

Every (3,2)(3,2)-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, let GG be a counter-example of minimum order. Obviously, GG is connected.

Claim 7.1

We have δ⁡(G)=2\delta(G)=2.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exists a vertex uu in GG such that d⁡(u)=1d(u)=1. The graph G−uG-u is (3,2)(3,2)-saturated subcubic such that g3​(G−u)=3g_{3}(G-u)=3. Then, G−uG-u is (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable. Hence, either 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} is not assigned to the neighbor of uu. By coloring uu using the appropriate color 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} we obtain a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Claim 7.2

There are no adjacent two 22-vertices in GG.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that there exist two 22-vertices u,v∈V⁡(G)u,v\in V(G) that are adjacent. Let u1u_{1} (resp., v1v_{1}) be the other neighbor of uu (resp., vv). Let u2u_{2} and u3u_{3} (resp., v2v_{2} and v3v_{3}) be the other neighbors of u1u_{1} (resp., v1v_{1}) when they exist. As g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3, u1,u2,u3u_{1},u_{2},u_{3} (resp., v1,v2,v3v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}) form a cycle when they exist. Let u4u_{4} (resp., u5u_{5}) be the other neighbor of u2u_{2} (resp., u3u_{3}). Consider the graph G′G^{\prime} obtained by deleting uu from GG and adding an edge between u1u_{1} and vv. Clearly, G′G^{\prime} is (3,2)(3,2)-saturated subcubic such that g3​(G′)=3g_{3}(G^{\prime})=3. Consider a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of G′G^{\prime}. If one of the colors 1a1_{a} or 1b1_{b} is not assigned to neither of the vertices u1u_{1} nor vv, by coloring uu using this color we obtain a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG, which is a contradiction. So, we may assume that u1u_{1} is colored by 1a1_{a} and vv is colored by 1b1_{b}. If 1b1_{b} is not assigned to neither of the vertices u2u_{2} and u3u_{3}, then we can recolor u1u_{1} by 1b1_{b} and uu by 1a1_{a} to obtain a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG, which is a contradiction. So, we may assume that u2u_{2} is colored by 1b1_{b} and u3u_{3} is colored by 3a3_{a}. Similarly, we may assume that v1v_{1}, v2v_{2}, and v3v_{3} are colored by 1a1_{a}, 1b1_{b}, and 3b3_{b}, respectively. If u4u_{4} is not colored by 1a1_{a}, then we can recolor u2u_{2} by 1a1_{a}, u1u_{1} by 1b1_{b}, and uu by 1a1_{a} to obtain a contradiction. Hence, u4u_{4} is colored by 1a1_{a}. If u5u_{5} is colored by 3k3_{k}, for some k∈{b,c}k\in\{b,c\}, then we can recolor u3u_{3} by 1a1_{a}, u1u_{1} by 3a3_{a}, and uu by 1a1_{a} to obtain a contradiction. Thus, u5u_{5} is colored by 1k1_{k}, for some k∈{a,b}k\in\{a,b\}. Therefore, neither of the vertices that are at a distance of at most 33 from uu is colored by 3c3_{c}. By assigning 3c3_{c} to uu we obtain a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG, a contradiction. ∎

Let TT be a set of vertices that contains exactly one vertex from each triangle in GG and suppose that TT is chosen with minimum cardinality. That is, every vertex in TT belongs to a triangle in GG and neither of the other vertices of this triangle belongs to TT. In addition, suppose that TT is chosen with the maximum number of 22-vertices; among all choices, TT is chosen with the maximum number of non-heavy 33-vertices. Let RR be the sungraph induced by V⁡(G)∖TV(G)\setminus T. Clearly, Δ⁡(R)≤2\Delta(R)\leq 2. Our goal is to prove that the vertices of TT can be colored using the colors 3a,3b,3c3_{a},3_{b},3_{c}. Then, we will prove that in every odd cycle in RR, there exists a vertex that is at a distance less than four from at most two vertices in TT. Moreover, such vertices in every odd cycle are at a distance of at least four from each other. Then, we will color the vertices of RR using the colors 1a,1b,3k1_{a},1_{b},3_{k}, where 3k3_{k} is used for one vertex from each odd cycle. Therefore, the 3k3_{k} color will be properly chosen from 3a,3b,3c3_{a},3_{b},3_{c} in order to obtain a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG, which is a contradiction.
We will start by studying the relations between the vertices in G3​[T]G^{3}[T].

Claim 7.3

If x∈Tx\in T is a 22-vertex, then dG3​[T]​(x)≤2d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)\leq 2.

Proof.

Let x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} be the neighbors of xx. By Claim 7.2, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are 33-vertices. Let y1y_{1} (resp., y2y_{2}) be the neighbor of x1x_{1} (resp., x2x_{2}) other than xx and x2x_{2} (resp., x1x_{1}). Let i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. If yiy_{i} is a 33-vertex, then yiy_{i} belongs to a triangle, which at most one of its vertices belongs to TT. Similarly, if yiy_{i} is a 22-vertex, then the neighbor of yiy_{i} other than xix_{i} belongs to a triangle, which at most one of its vertices belongs to TT. Hence, there is at most one vertex ziz_{i} in TT at a distance of at most 33 from xx such that the shortest x​zixz_{i}-path passes through yiy_{i}. Thus, dG3​[T]​(x)≤2d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)\leq 2. ∎

Claim 7.4

If x∈Tx\in T is a non-heavy 33-vertex, then dG3​[T]​(x)≤3d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)\leq 3.

Proof.

Let x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} be the neighbors of xx such that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are adjacent. As TT is chosen with the maximum number of 22-vertices, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are 33-vertices. As xx is not heavy, x3x_{3} is a 22-vertex. Let i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}. As in Claim 7.3, at most one vertex in TT such that the shortest path from xx to this vertex passes through xix_{i} is at a distance of at most 33 from xx. Thus, dG3​[T]​(x)≤3d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)\leq 3. ∎

Remark 7.1

Let x∈Tx\in T be a non-heavy 33-vertex such that dG3​[T]​(x)=3d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)=3. Let x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} be the neighbors of xx in GG and y,z,wy,z,w be the neighbors of xx in G3​[T]G^{3}[T]. Suppose that the shortest x​yxy-path (resp., x​zxz-path, x​wxw-path) passes through x1x_{1} (resp., x2x_{2}, x3x_{3}). Denote by y1y_{1} (resp., z1,w1z_{1},w_{1}) the vertex in the triangle containing yy (resp., z,wz,w) that is the closest, among the vertices of the triangle, to xx. Note that y1y_{1} (resp., z1z_{1}, w1w_{1}) may be yy (resp., zz, ww). Then, the shortest x1​y1x_{1}y_{1}-path (resp., x2​z1x_{2}z_{1}-path) is either an edge or a path of length two, where the second vertex is a 22-vertex. Moreover, the shortest x3​w1x_{3}w_{1}-path is an edge.

Claim 7.5

If x∈Tx\in T is a heavy vertex, then dG3​[T]​(x)≤4d_{G^{3}[T]}(x)\leq 4. Moreover, three of the vertices that are adjacent to xx in G3​[T]G^{3}[T] are 22-vertices.

Proof.

Let x1,x2,x3x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} be the neighbors of xx such that x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are adjacent. As TT is chosen with the maximum number of 22-vertices, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are 33-vertices. Similarly, as TT is chosen with the maximum number of non-heavy 33-vertices, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are heavy. Thus, x3x_{3} is not heavy. Let uu and vv be the neighbors of x3x_{3} other than xx, such that uu is a 22-vertex. Hence, u∈Tu\in T and d​i​s​tG​(x,u)=2dist_{G}(x,u)=2. Moreover, the third neighbor of vv, which may be in TT, is at a distance 33 from xx. On the other hand, let y1y_{1} (resp., y2y_{2}) be the third neighbor of x1x_{1} (resp., x2x_{2}). Let i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. Again, yiy_{i} is not heavy, then the triangle containing yiy_{i} contains a 22-vertex called ziz_{i}. We have d​i​s​tG​(x,zi)=3dist_{G}(x,z_{i})=3. The result follows. ∎

Claim 7.6

G3​[T]G^{3}[T] contains a complete subgraph of order 44 if and only if G3​[T]=K4G^{3}[T]=K_{4}.

Proof.

Suppose that G3​[T]G^{3}[T] contains a complete subgraph of order 44 and let x,y,z,wx,y,z,w be its vertices. By Claims 7.3, 7.4, and 7.5, x,y,z,wx,y,z,w are non-heavy 33-vertices. Applying Remark 7.1 to x,y,z,wx,y,z,w, we can deduce T={x,y,z,w}T=\{x,y,z,w\}. The result follows. ∎

First, suppose that G3​[T]=K4G^{3}[T]=K_{4}.

Assertion 7.1

GG is (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

This case is represented in Figure 1. Suppose that the red x1​y1x_{1}y_{1}-path is of length 22. Color xx and y2y_{2} by 3a3_{a}, z2z_{2} by 3b3_{b}, and w2w_{2} by 3c3_{c}. The remaining vertices form a bipartite graph, so we can color them by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b}. Now, assume that the red x1​y1x_{1}y_{1}-path and x2​z1x_{2}z_{1}-path are of length one. As GG is (3,2)(3,2)-saturated, either y2y_{2} or y3y_{3} is not heavy. Assume that y3y_{3} is not heavy. Hence, the red y3​z2y_{3}z_{2}-path is of length 22. Color xx by 3a3_{a}, y1y_{1} and z3z_{3} by 3b3_{b}, and w1w_{1} by 3c3_{c}. Again, we can color the remaining vertices by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b}. The last case is when y3y_{3} is heavy. Hence, z2z_{2} is heavy and z3z_{3} is not heavy. This case is similar to the previous one. ∎

So, we may assume that G3​[T]G^{3}[T] does not contain a complete subgraph of order 44.

Claim 7.7

The graph G3​[T]G^{3}[T] is 33-colorable.

Proof.

Let HH be the set of heavy vertices in TT (they belong to TT but are heavy in GG). By Claim 7.5, every vertex in HH is adjacent in G3​[T]G^{3}[T] to three vertices of degree 22 in G3​[T]G^{3}[T]. Let H′H^{\prime} be the set of vertices of degree 22 in G3​[T]G^{3}[T] that are adjacent in G3​[T]G^{3}[T] to a vertex in HH. As G3​[T]−H′G^{3}[T]-H^{\prime} has maximum degree 33 and no complete subgraph of order 44, by Brooks’ Theorem, G3​[T]−H′G^{3}[T]-H^{\prime} is 33-colorable. A 33-coloring of G3​[T]−H′G^{3}[T]-H^{\prime} can be easily extended to G3​[T]G^{3}[T] since a 2-vertex in G3​[T]G^{3}[T] has at most two neighbors in G3​[T]G^{3}[T]. ∎

Let CC be an odd cycle in RR. Obviously, CC is of order of at least 55. Moreover, CC contains a 22-vertex. Let XX be a set formed by taking exactly one 22-vertex from every odd cycle in RR.

Claim 7.8

Let x∈Xx\in X. At most two vertices in TT are at a distance less than 44 from xx.

Proof.

Let uu and vv be the neighbors of xx. By Claim 7.2, uu and vv are 33-vertices. Let u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} (resp., v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}) be the other neighbors of uu (resp., vv). Then, u1​u2,v1​v2∈E⁡(G)u_{1}u_{2},v_{1}v_{2}\in E(G). Suppose that u1u_{1} and v1v_{1} belong to the odd cycle in RR that contains xx. Then, u2,v2∈Tu_{2},v_{2}\in T. Hence, u2u_{2} and v2v_{2} are non-heavy vertices. Thus, u2u_{2} (resp., v2v_{2}) is not adjacent to a vertex in TT. Moreover, the third neighbor of u1u_{1} (resp., v1v_{1}) belongs to the odd cycle in RR that contains xx. That is, it does not belong to TT. The result follows. ∎

Claim 7.9

Let x,y∈Xx,y\in X. Then, d​i​s​tG​(x,y)≥4dist_{G}(x,y)\geq 4.

Proof.

Let u,v,u1,u2,v1,v2u,v,u_{1},u_{2},v_{1},v_{2} be the vertices defined in Claim 7.8. Clearly, y∉{u,v,u1,u2,v1,v2}y\notin\{u,v,u_{1},\\ u_{2},v_{1},v_{2}\}. Let u3u_{3} (resp., v3v_{3}) be the third neighbor of u2u_{2} (resp., v2v_{2}). Now, u3u_{3} and v3v_{3} are 22-vertices. Then, dR​(u3)≤1d_{R}(u_{3})\leq 1 and dR​(v3)≤1d_{R}(v_{3})\leq 1. Thus, y∉{u3,v3}y\notin\{u_{3},v_{3}\}. The result follows. ∎

Now, color the vertices of TT by 3a,3b,3c3_{a},3_{b},3_{c}. Note that, R−XR-X is bipartite. So, color the vertices of R−XR-X by 1a1_{a} and 1b1_{b}. Finally, for each x∈Xx\in X, there exists a color 3k∈{3a,3b,3c}3_{k}\in\{3_{a},3_{b},3_{c}\} that can be properly assigned to xx. Then a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring of GG is obtained, a contradiction. ∎

5 Sharpness of the Results and Open Problems

We proved that a 00-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 admits both a (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing coloring and a (2,2,2,2,3)(2,2,2,2,3)-packing coloring, except 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1}. Both results are sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable and others that are not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 1).

Proposition 1

The graph 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} (resp., 𝒢4\mathcal{G}_{4}) is not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable (resp., (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable).

Proof.

The diameter of 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} is 22, then at most one vertex can be colored by a color 22. Moreover, in 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1}, there are no independent set of order 44. Thus, at most five vertices can be colored using the colors 1,2a,2b1,2_{a},2_{b}. Therefore, 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1} is not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable. Similarly, at most four vertices of 𝒢4\mathcal{G}_{4} can be colored using four different colors 22. Then, 𝒢4\mathcal{G}_{4} is not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable. ∎

We proved that a 00-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 has χρ​(G)≤6\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 6. We did not find such a graph GG such that χρ​(G)≥5\chi_{\rho}(G)\geq 5. Thus, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 1

If GG is a 00-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4, then χρ​(G)≤4\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 4.

We proved that a 11-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,3,k)(1,1,3,k)-packing colorable for all k≥3k\geq 3. The result is sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (1,1,3)(1,1,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 2) and there are such graphs that are not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 3).

Proposition 2

The graph 𝒢5\mathcal{G}_{5} is not (1,1,3)(1,1,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary that 𝒢5\mathcal{G}_{5} is (1,1,3)(1,1,3)-packing colorable. Each odd cycle must contain a vertex colored by 33. Let x,y,zx,y,z be vertices in the three triangles that are colored by 33. Clearly, neither of x,y,zx,y,z belongs to the cycle of order 99. Thus, the cycle of order 99 contains a fourth vertex colored by 33, which is at a distance less than 33 from one of the vertices x,y,zx,y,z, a contradiction. ∎

Proposition 3

The graph 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2} (resp., 𝒢6\mathcal{G}_{6}) is not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable (resp., (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable).

Proof.

The graph 𝒢2\mathcal{G}_{2} is obviously not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable. Suppose to the contrary that the graph 𝒢6\mathcal{G}_{6} has a (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing coloring. Let x,y,zx,y,z (resp., x′,y′,z′x^{\prime},y^{\prime},z^{\prime}) be the vertices of the first (resp., second) triangle. Let uu be the vertex having a common neighbor on the two triangles and u1u_{1} (resp., u2u_{2}) be the other vertex having a neighbor in the first (resp., second) triangle. As each triangle contains three colors, uu and u1u_{1} (resp., uu and u2u_{2}) have the same color. Thus, u1u_{1} and u2u_{2} have the same color, a contradiction. ∎

We proved that a 11-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in several senses: there are such graphs that are not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 3), there are such graphs that are not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 3), and there is a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 that is not (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 4).

Proposition 4

The graph 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} is not (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} has (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing coloring. Note that the diameter of 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} is 33, then at most one vertex can be colored by 33. If three of the cycle of order 66 are colored by 11, then no more vertices are colored by 11. In this case, at most four of the remaining vertices can be colored by the two colors 22, a contradiction. If at most two vertices of the cycle of order 66 are colored by 11, then at most five of the remaining vertices can be colored by the two colors 22 and the color 11, a contradiction. ∎

We proved that a 11-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (2,2,2,2,3)(2,2,2,2,3)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 3).

In addition, we pose the following problems.

Problem 1

Is every 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 (1,2,3,3)(1,2,3,3)-packing colorable? (1,2,2,4)(1,2,2,4)-packing colorable? (2,2,2,2,4)(2,2,2,2,4)-packing colorable?

We proved that a 11-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 has χρ​(G)≤6\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 6. We did not find such a graph GG such that χρ​(G)≥6\chi_{\rho}(G)\geq 6. Thus, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 2

If GG is a 11-saturated subcubic graph such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3, then χρ​(G)≤5\chi_{\rho}(G)\leq 5.

We proved that every 11-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in several senses: there are 11-saturated subcubic graphs such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 that are not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 5), there are 11-saturated subcubic graphs such that g3​(G)≥5g_{3}(G)\geq 5 that are not (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 6), and there is a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)≤4g_{3}(G)\leq 4 that is not (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 7).

Proposition 5

The graph 𝒢7\mathcal{G}_{7} is not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that 𝒢7\mathcal{G}_{7} has a (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing coloring. At most three vertices ar colored by 11. If three vertices ar colored by 11, then the remaining vertices are at a distance 22 from each other. Thus, they cannot be colored using only two colors 22, a contradiction. Otherwise, at most two vertices are colored by 11, then at most two of the remaining vertices can be colored by the same color 22, say 2a2_{a}. The remaining vertices are at a distance 22 from each other, then they cannot be colored by 2b2_{b}, a contradiction. ∎

Proposition 6

The graph 𝒢8\mathcal{G}_{8} is not (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that 𝒢8\mathcal{G}_{8} has a (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring. Then, at least two 33-vertices are colored by two different colors 22. Suppose that xx and yy are two non-adjacent 33-vertices that are colored by 2a2_{a} and 2b2_{b}, respectively. The remaining six vertices cannot be colored by 2a2_{a} or 2b2_{b}. It is clear that they cannot be colored by 11 and 2c2_{c} only, a contradiction. ∎

Proposition 7

The graph 𝒢9\mathcal{G}_{9} is not (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that 𝒢9\mathcal{G}_{9} has a (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing coloring. As a cycle of order 55 is not (1,2,2)(1,2,2)-packing colorable, the vertices of the cycle of order 55 that contains four 33-vertices must uses the four colors 1,2a,2b,2c1,2_{a},2_{b},2_{c}. The two remaining vertices are at a distance of at most 22 from the vertices of the mentioned cycle. Then, they are colored by the color 11. But at least one of their neighbors is colored by 11, a contradiction. ∎

We proved that every 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 8) and there are such graphs that are not (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 4). Moreover, as we did not find a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)≥4g_{3}(G)\geq 4 that is not (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 3

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph is (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable.

Proposition 8

The graph 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} is not (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

The diameter of 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} is 33, then at most one vertex can be colored by 3a3_{a} (resp., 3b3_{b}). But there are three disjoint triangles that must contain a vertex of color 33. Thus, 𝒢10\mathcal{G}_{10} does not have a (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing coloring. ∎

We proved that every 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in several senses: there are such graphs that are not (1,2,2,3)(1,2,2,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 4), there are such graphs that are not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 1), and there is a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=4g_{3}(G)=4 that is not (1,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 7). In addition, we did not find a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=4g_{3}(G)=4 that is not (1,2,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable. Thus, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 4

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph is (1,2,2,2,2)(1,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

We proved that every 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in several senses: there are such graphs that are not (2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 1) and there is a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g4​(G)=4g_{4}(G)=4 that is not (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable (Proposition 9). Moreover, we did not find a 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 that is not (2,2,2,2,3)(2,2,2,2,3)-packing colorable. Thus, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 5

Every 22-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (2,2,2,2,3)(2,2,2,2,3)-packing colorable.

Proposition 9

The graph 𝒢9\mathcal{G}_{9} is not (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable.

Proof.

On the contrary, suppose that 𝒢9\mathcal{G}_{9} has a (2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2)-packing coloring. A cycle of order 55 must be colored by the five colors 22. The two remaining vertices are at a distance of at most 22 from any vertex of the mentioned cycle, a contradiction. ∎

We proved that every (3,0)(3,0)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,2,4)(1,1,2,4)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 8). In addition, we did not find such a graph that is not (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable. So, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 6

Every (3,0)(3,0)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,2)(1,1,2)-packing colorable.

We proved that every (3,1)(3,1)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in the sense that there are such graphs that are not (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 8).

We proved that every (3,2)(3,2)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 is (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable. The result is sharp in several sense: there are such graphs that are not (1,1,3,3)(1,1,3,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 8) and there is a (3,3)(3,3)-saturated subcubic graph GG that is not (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable (Proposition 10).

Proposition 10

The graph 𝒢11\mathcal{G}_{11} is not (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable.

Proof.

The diameter of 𝒢11\mathcal{G}_{11} is 33, then at most one vertex can be colored by 3a3_{a} (resp., 3b,3c3_{b},3_{c}). But there are four disjoint triangles that must contain a vertex of color 33. Thus, 𝒢11\mathcal{G}_{11} does not have a (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing coloring. ∎

Although we found a (3,3)(3,3)-saturated subcubic graph GG such that g3​(G)=3g_{3}(G)=3 that is not (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable, we think it may be the unique counter-example. Thus, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 7

Every claw-free subcubic graph, except 𝒢11\mathcal{G}_{11}, is (1,1,3,3,3)(1,1,3,3,3)-packing colorable.

We also conjecture the following.

Conjecture 8

Every claw-free subcubic graph is (1,1,2,3)(1,1,2,3)-packing colorable.

Conjecture 9

Every claw-free subcubic graph is (2,2,2,2,2,2,2)(2,2,2,2,2,2,2)-packing colorable.
